Review Body:
Strong, evidence-based book that avoids drawing sweeping conclusions (like that all social media, video games, or porn are bad) but that asserts that a significant tech change is happening and that serious, coordinated responses are needed.

Haidt argues that parents and society have both over-protected children and young people in the real world, while simultaneously under-protecting children and young people online. This has resulted in a mental health crisis and a “great rewiring” of an entire generation’s adolescence via its’ migration online.

I really appreciate how reasonable and common-sense Haidt makes his solutions: broad, but actionable. There are some policy suggestions for government, but most things are actionable by parents and families in the grassroots and culture, and even individual choices. Rather than vague nostrums or demanding a major commitment to activism, there’s a lot of middle ground here for a parent to choose from depending on their level of time and agency. Even if no policy-level changes occurred, Haidt seems to provide a roadmap to where about 90% plus of the damage done by the “Great Re-wiring” could be reduced through a household’s intentional planning.

As an educator and parent, reading this book was like getting the answers to the test. Or seeing an X-ray of what’s going on everyday in my life. I can’t think of a book that has resonated more with my lived experience in the last 10 years than this text. I am seeing the things he is describing here almost every minute of every day. My school is starting to come around on this issue and we’re already seeing radically different results. I think the revolution is now.

Review Body:
I don't exactly fit the target audience for this book. I'm a parent, yes, but an empty-nester. And one who's just a little too glued to her smartphone to ever feel at ease reading about the darker side of a device that's come to feel as essential as air. But I dare you -- parent or not -- to read the introduction of Jonathan Haidt's The Anxious Generation and NOT find yourself as engrossed as I was in this book. If by slim chance you aren't, go read some social media. You'll suddenly see the light in your mind's eye as clear and bright as a laser's.

The Anxious Generation waves a big red flag over the ubiquitous and unbridled use of smartphones and social media, particularly by the generation who entered adolescence while using them -- Generation Z, those born between 1995 and 2010. Its main premise is that Gen Z is now experiencing not just a spike but an epidemic of depression, anxiety, self-harm and suicide, due largely to a lack of legal limits placed on tech companies to protect young, formative minds. Haidt, a social psychologist, presents plenty of mental health data to back up his claim, and describes in detail "four foundational harms" that he says have impacted the development of Gen Z's social and emotional cognitive abilities. He tells us why social media harms more girls than boys, and why the virtual world of video gaming and the internet's limitless access to hardcore porn have created boys who are not only lonelier than those of previous generations, but also more reluctant to grow up. As if that weren't enough, Haidt adds that a "phone-based life produces a spiritual degradation, not just in adolescents, but in all of us." That's why this book is for everyone, even an empty-nester like me.

This book is a true wake-up call on -- let's face it -- a tool most of us can no longer even imagine living without. That's why its last section is arguably its most important. In it, Haidt offers the many steps he feels must be taken by federal and state governments, tech companies, parents and schools to prevent continued harm to preteens. Because smartphones, he says, present inherent social traps, solving a social dilemma of this magnitude requires real collective action. If I were still raising a formative mind under my own roof, I'd be taking very careful note of EVERY. SINGLE. STEP. And not just those aimed at parents.

I gave this book a 5-star rating because its topic is timely, alarming and important. As Haidt mentions, this problem is one that won't just affect one generation, but all those who follow. (And as long as my aging mind can still pick up new tricks on my smartphone, why on earth would I ever think some of the dangers don't apply to me?) I do have one serious gripe about the book, however. Haidt strongly encourages parents to give kids more unsupervised time exploring their neighborhoods. "The need for risky play," he calls it. Although I grasp his reasoning, this argument is one I cannot wholly endorse. I think anyone who has ever, like me, had to have a security guard drag a stalker away in a mall would understand, even if it happened 50 years ago.

Review Body:
COMMENTS ABOUT JONATHAN HAIDT’S THE ANXIOUS GENERATION

Well researched and documented. Practical, timely, and relevant. Deeper than one might expect. Well written and readable.

Haidt’s book is especially well written. His illustrations make sense. Paragraphing is organized. Explanations are clear. Case studies are brief and obvious.

It is also helpful with its suggestions for governments, schools, and parents. And who can’t identify with the generally real life examples that clarify Haidt’s points? The scope, gravity, and description of the mental health crisis borders on overkill.

Something that impressed me was the depth of explanation of the dual problem—what Haidt refers to as the two whales: smartphone abuse and lack of normal play for children. I am old enough to see both problems as they developed, but they sneaked by me. Well said, Jonathan Haidt!

Footnotes and references abound in this work. There are 30 pages of each. Add a substantial index.

I recommend that any caring parent take time to read at least the introduction and at least parts of the first and second chapters. Some time in chapter 12 is also advisable—“What Parents Can Do Now”. It is college level reading.

Haidt is an atheist, but his comments regarding the importance of religion for good mental health are noteworthy. Chapter 8.

I finished this book jaded against big tech and social media. Instagram recently sent this message: “Parents want to feel confident that their teens can use social media to connect with their friends and explore their interests without having to worry about unsafe or inappropriate experiences. That's why Instagram recently introduced teen accounts with built-in limits. Users between the ages of 13 and 17 are now automatically enrolled in Instagram teen accounts. Teens under 16 will need parental permission to change these settings. To learn more, visit instagram.com/teenaccounts.” I am thinking, “Too little, too late.” This seems more like damage control. Also, will their teen accounts really work? What proof of age is there?

This book focuses on what is going on with children regarding smartphone use. As we enter the age of AI, I wonder what is happening with ADULTS and their Internet contraptions and with their mental well-being.

It reaffirmed why our school is proudly a non-phone school. The research and insights in this book are a sobering reminder of how technology is reshaping childhood—and not always for the better.

This perspective on how phones and screens are fueling anxiety in children hit home. It’s not just about removing phones during the school day but about taking a stand to preserve play, curiosity, and mental health. This book has inspired me to double down on educating parents about the importance of creating boundaries around screen time. It’s not just about what happens in the classroom; it’s about fostering a village-wide commitment to protecting childhood.

If you haven’t picked this up yet, it’s an absolute must-read for 2024 (and honestly, every year after). The anuthor’s actionable advice and deep understanding of the challenges we’re facing today make this book a game-changer. Whether you're a teacher, a parent, or simply someone passionate about the next generation, The Anxious Generation is a call to action we all need to hear.

Review Body:
An essential read for parents and educators and a fantastic read for even a curious mind.

Haidt's analysis was useful in getting a better idea of what it's like to grow up plugged in. I'm 33 and I was in a time where we weren't quite as plugged in as we are now. However, I was able to relate to the chapters which informed of parents being afraid to let their kids explore away from home. I wasn't really able to do that much. About as far as my parents allowed were the beginning of our neighborhood at my friends home.

This continued into my 20's when my parents still had a curfew for me to get home at night and before a certain time.

As a event coordinator sometimes offering classes, I will use this knowledge to craft classes that are not so screen driven when I can. I highly recommend this book!
